mappings.note: Ten conical tents: curved surface area of one cone, scaled and costed against a 2 m wide canvas. A single basic solid repeated, never combined with another.

Cone carved out of a cube: surface of the remainder = cube surface MINUS the circular base PLUS the cone's curved surface. Adding and subtracting component areas of a composite - LO-2, and the volume twin of this item sits elsewhere.
Two separate spheres: volume ratio gives r : R, then (R - r) : r. Pure comparison, no combination.
Cylinder melted and recast into conical toys; the count follows from equating volumes across the shape change.
Volume of the largest cone cut from a cube. Only the cone is wanted, so no subtraction from the cube and no melting.
Sand tipped from a cylindrical bucket into a conical heap - the same material takes a new shape, and the slant height is the follow-up. Conversion, not combination.
Cylinder with a hemisphere at each end, volumes added, with the caps consuming 2r of the total height. Volume of a combination.
Two spheres melted into one, with mass standing in for volume because the metal is the same. Still a recast, so C-7.3-LO-3.
Hemispherical depression cut into a cube: surface = cube - pi r^2 + 2 pi r^2. The subtract-then-add of component areas is the heart of LO-2.
Hollow hemispherical vessel painted ALL OVER: outer curved + inner curved + the annular rim. Assembling three component areas of one composite body, then costing it.
Pipe flow filling a tank: a long cylinder of water becomes a slab in a wider cylinder. Volume conserved across shapes over a stated time.
Pipe flow filling a cuboidal pond, solved for time. Duplicate stem of the 2-mark item earlier in the chapter, mapped consistently to the conversion outcome.
Cylinder surmounted by a cone whose 90-degree vertical angle fixes l; total surface area of the combined toy. LO-2 rather than LO-3 because no volume is asked.

Two steps, two outcomes: the leftover metal is a cylinder minus two hemispheres (C-7.2-LO-3), and that leftover is then drawn into a wire (C-7.3-LO-3). Citing only the recast would hide where the source volume comes from.
Milk from a cylindrical tanker split into a cuboidal and a cylindrical vessel; levels follow from the transferred volumes taking new shapes.

Revolving a right triangle about its hypotenuse makes a DOUBLE CONE, and the item asks for both its volume (LO-3) and its surface (LO-2), the two cones sharing a base circle that is not exposed. Both outcomes are genuinely exercised.

Iron pole = a wide cylinder with a narrower cylinder on top; volumes added, then converted to mass. Volume of a combination. (Stem says 'mass of the pipe' although the solid described is a solid pole.)
Hemisphere-plus-cone toy volume, then the difference against a circumscribing cylinder - two composite volumes compared. LO-3 throughout; no surface area is asked.
The combined volume is GIVEN and the height is the unknown (LO-3 worked backwards); the second half then costs the painting of the hemispherical part only (LO-2). Both halves are needed.
Circus tent = cylinder plus cone; canvas is the two curved surfaces, with the cone's height taken from the total height. Surface of a combination.
One conical heap: volume, then curved surface for the canvas. Two formulas on the same single solid, so competency level rather than a combination outcome.
Well embankment case study: cylindrical earth respread as an annular ring, width unknown. Conversion of one solid shape into another.
Canal case study: a moving cuboidal column of water becomes standing water over a field. Volume conserved across shapes.

Part (i) is a plain disc, one cylinder (C-7.2); part (ii) is a captab, a cylinder with a hemisphere at each end whose volume must be assembled (C-7.2-LO-3). The contrast between the two shapes is the question.
Silo case study asks both the metal SHEET (curved cylinder + curved cone, LO-2, then costed) and the storage CAPACITY (LO-3). Two parts, two outcomes, so both are cited.
